findings.note: Flaky (and currently failing) test on a frozen branch: TestCodexJudgeStopsOnCancellation asserts f.calls < MaxAttempts, but codexClock()'s After channel is pre-filled, so codex.go's `select { case <-ctx.Done(): ...; case <-j.clock.After(...): }` has two ready cases and Go chooses uniformly at random. When the timer arm wins five times the ladder runs to completion and the test fails. Measured ~10% failure rate (4-9 failures per 50 runs over 15 batches), and it failed during a plain `go test ./internal/fsm/judge/...`, which also dropped package coverage to 99.8% under the repo's 100% rule. This is not only a test defect: the property the test names — a cancelled caller stops the ladder — is not guaranteed by the source, which should check ctx.Err() before selecting on the timer.

findings.note: peek() loads an entire run's audit.jsonl into memory (deps.ReadFile is os.ReadFile with no cap) purely to read its first line, then truncates. A long-lived run's log is unbounded; a bounded read of the first run.MaxLine bytes would be equivalent and cheap.

evidence.note: ReadFile of runs/<id>/audit.jsonl before the MaxLine truncation

findings.note: ctxDeps.git discards git's stderr, so every wrapped failure (rootOf, toplevel) reports a generic 'not inside a git repository' with no underlying git message, making misconfiguration harder to diagnose.

findings.note: nonce() panics on a crypto/rand failure and no production path recovers (the only recover() in the tree is in cli_test.go), so the CLI would crash with a stack trace instead of the structured ERR_INTERNAL envelope. crypto/rand.Read does not fail on supported platforms, and the behaviour is deliberately covered by a test, so this is accepted rather than a defect.
